title: The Raven
paragraphs: There was once a queen who had a little daughter, still too small to walk by herself. One day the child was very fussy, and no matter what the mother did, she could not quiet her. She lost her patience, and when she saw the ravens flying around the castle, she opened the window and said, “I wish you were a raven and would fly away, so I could have a little peace.” The words had barely left her mouth when the child in her arms turned into a raven and flew out of the open window. The bird flew to a dark forest and stayed there a long time, and in all that while the parents heard nothing of their child.

Long afterward, a man was making his way through the forest when he heard a raven calling, and he followed the sound of its voice. As he came closer, the raven said, “I am a king’s daughter by birth, but I am under some enchantment now. You can set me free, though.” “What must I do?” he asked. She answered, “Go deeper into the forest until you come to a house where an old woman lives. She will offer you food and drink, but you must take neither. If you do, you will fall into a deep sleep and won’t be able to help me. In the garden behind the house there is a big heap of tanbark, and you must stand on it and watch for me. I will drive up in my carriage at two o’clock in the afternoon for three days in a row. The first day it will be pulled by four white horses, the second day by four chestnut horses, and the last by four black ones. But if you fail to stay awake and I find you asleep, I will not be set free.”

The man promised to do everything she asked, but the raven said, “Alas, I already know that you will accept something from the woman, and then you won’t be able to save me.” Again he assured her that under no circumstances would he touch any food or drink.
When he arrived at the house and stepped inside, the old woman came to meet him. “You poor man, you look so tired!” she said. “Come in and rest, and let me give you something to eat and drink.”
“No,” the man answered, “I won’t eat or drink anything.”
But she wouldn’t leave him be. She kept pressing him: “If you won’t eat, you could at least have a glass of wine. One drink is nothing.” In the end he let himself be talked into it, and he drank.

As the appointed hour drew near, he went out into the garden and climbed onto the tan-heap to wait for the raven. Suddenly a heaviness came over him that he couldn’t fight off. He lay down for just a little while, fully determined to stay awake, but within a minute his eyes had closed by themselves, and he sank into a sleep so deep that nothing in the world could have woken him. At two o’clock the raven came driving up, pulled by her four white horses. Before she even arrived, she sighed and said to herself, “I know he has fallen asleep.” When she reached the garden, she found him just as she had feared, lying on the tan-heap, sound asleep. She climbed down from her carriage and went to him. She called his name and shook him, but it was no use. He kept on sleeping.

At noon the next day the old woman came to him again with food and drink, and again he turned them down at first. But she begged so persistently that he finally gave in, picked up the glass, and drank once more.

Around two o’clock he went out to the garden and onto the tan-heap to watch for the raven. He hadn’t been there long when he grew so tired that his legs could hardly hold him and he couldn’t stand up any longer. So he lay down again and fell fast asleep. The raven came driving up with her four chestnut horses, and she said sadly to herself, “I know he has fallen asleep.” She went to look for him as before, but he slept on, and there was no waking him.
The day after, the old woman said to him, “What’s the matter with you? You aren’t eating or drinking anything. Do you want to kill yourself?”
He answered, “I mustn’t, and I won’t, eat or drink.”
But she set the dish of food and the glass of wine down in front of him, and when he caught the smell of the wine, he couldn’t hold out against the temptation. He took a long drink.

When the hour came around again, he went out as usual to the tan-heap in the garden to wait for the king’s daughter. But he felt even more weighed down by weariness than on the two days before, and he threw himself down and slept like a log. At two o’clock the raven came into sight, and this time her coachman and everything about her, horses included, were black.

She was sadder than ever as she drove up, and she said mournfully, “I know he has fallen asleep, and he won’t be able to set me free.” She found him sleeping heavily, and nothing she did could wake him. So she laid beside him a loaf of bread, some meat, and a flask of wine, the kind that never runs out, however much he takes from it. Then she pulled a gold ring off her finger, with her name engraved on it, and slid it onto one of his. Last of all, she left a letter beside him. In it she told him exactly what food and drink she had left for him, and she ended with these words: “I see that as long as you stay here, you will never be able to set me free. But if you still want to, come to the golden castle of Stromberg. It is well within your power to do that.” Then she went back to her carriage and drove off to the golden castle of Stromberg.

When the man woke up and realized he had been asleep, his heart sank. “She must have come and driven away again,” he said, “and now it’s too late for me to save her.” Then he noticed the things lying beside him. He read the letter and understood everything that had happened. He got up at once, eager to set out for the castle of Stromberg, but he had no idea which way to go. He wandered for a long time looking for it, and at last he came to a dark forest. He kept walking through it for fourteen days and still couldn’t find his way out. Night fell once more, and, worn out, he lay down under a bush and went to sleep. The next day he went on through the forest again, and that evening, hoping to rest, he lay down as before, but there was such howling and wailing that he couldn’t sleep. He waited until it was darker and people had started lighting the lamps in their houses. Then he saw a faint glimmer ahead of him and walked toward it.

The light came from a house, which looked smaller than it was because an enormous giant stood in front of it, towering over it. The man thought, “If the giant sees me go in, my life won’t be worth much.” Still, after a while he gathered his courage and went forward. When the giant saw him, he called out, “It’s lucky you’ve come. I haven’t had a bite to eat in ages. Now I can have you for supper.” “I’d rather you didn’t,” said the man, “because I’m not willing to be eaten. But if you’re hungry, I have enough to fill you up.” “In that case,” the giant replied, “I’ll leave you alone. I only thought of eating you because I had nothing else.”

So they went inside together and sat down, and the man took out the bread, the meat, and the wine, which, although he had eaten and drunk from them, were still undiminished. The giant was delighted with the fine meal and ate and drank until he was satisfied. When he had finished, the man asked whether he could tell him the way to the castle of Stromberg. “I’ll check my map,” the giant said. “All the towns, villages, and houses are marked on it.” He fetched the map and searched for the castle, but couldn’t find it. “Never mind,” he said. “I have bigger maps upstairs in the cupboard. We’ll look at those.” But they searched in vain, because the castle wasn’t marked on those either. The man now wanted to continue on his way, but the giant asked him to stay a day or two longer, until his brother came back from looking for food. When the brother got home, they asked him about the castle of Stromberg, and he said he would check his own maps as soon as he had eaten and taken the edge off his hunger. So when he had finished his supper, they all went up to his room together and went through his maps, but the castle wasn’t there. Then he brought out other, older maps, and they kept looking until at last they found it. It was many thousands of miles away. “How will I ever get there?” asked the man. “I have two hours to spare,” said the giant, “and I’ll carry you to somewhere near the castle. After that I have to go back and look after the child who is in our care.”

So the giant carried the man to within about a hundred leagues of the castle and set him down there. “You can walk the rest of the way yourself,” he said. The man traveled on, day and night, until he reached the golden castle of Stromberg. He found it standing on a glass mountain, and looking up from the bottom, he saw the enchanted maiden drive around her castle and then go inside. He was overjoyed to see her and longed to reach the top of the mountain, but its sides were so slippery that every time he tried to climb, he slid back down. When he saw that he could not get to her, he was deeply grieved. “I’ll stay here and wait for her,” he told himself. So he built a little hut and sat there watching for a whole year. Every day he saw the king’s daughter drive around her castle, and every day he was still unable to get any closer to her.

One day, looking out from his hut, he saw three robbers fighting, and he called out to them, “God be with you.” They stopped when they heard him, but they looked around and saw nobody, and went back to fighting even more fiercely than before. “God be with you,” he cried again. Again they paused and looked about, and seeing no one, returned to their fight. A third time he called out, “God be with you.” Then, wanting to know what the quarrel among the three men was about, he went out and asked why they were fighting each other so angrily. One of them said he had found a stick, and all he had to do was strike it against any door he wanted to go through, and the door would fly open. Another said he had found a cloak that made whoever wore it invisible. The third had caught a horse that would carry its rider over any obstacle, even up the glass mountain. They hadn’t been able to agree whether to stay together and share the things, or to part ways. When he heard this, the man said, “I’ll give you something in exchange for those three things. Not money, because I have none, but something worth far more. First, though, I have to test whether everything you’ve told me about them is true.” So the robbers made him get on the horse and handed him the stick and the cloak, and when he threw the cloak around himself, he couldn’t be seen anymore. Then he fell on them with the stick and beat them one after another, shouting, “There, you lazy good-for-nothings, you got what you deserve! Are you satisfied now?”

After that he rode up the glass mountain. When he reached the castle gate, he found it shut, but he struck it with his stick, and it flew wide open at once, and he went through. He climbed the steps and entered the room where the maiden sat with a golden goblet of wine in front of her. She couldn’t see him, because he was still wearing his cloak. He took the ring she had given him off his finger and threw it into the goblet, so that it rang as it hit the bottom. “That is my own ring!” she cried. “And if so, the man who is coming to set me free must be here too.”

She searched the castle for him but couldn’t find him anywhere. Meanwhile he had gone outside again, mounted his horse, and thrown off the cloak. So when she came to the castle gate, she saw him and cried out with joy. He dismounted and took her in his arms, and she kissed him and said, “Now you have truly set me free, and tomorrow we will celebrate our wedding.”
